*25. SHRI SANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of STATISTICS 
AND PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to enact a legislation to regulate 
recommendation, sanction and execution of projects under MPLADS; 
(b) whether existing guidelines are proposed to be amended; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) No, 
Sir. 
(b) and (c) The existing Guidelines on MPLADS have been revised and issued 
on 16 11.2005. The details thereof are given in the statement. 
Statement 
Detailed Guidelines on MPLADS 
Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) is under 
implementation since 1993-94. The Guidelines under the Scheme were revised 
from time to time and lastly it was revised in April, 2002. Subsequently, 
certain clariftcatory circulars have been issued. Now, a comprehensive 
revision has been made and a fresh set of Guidelines has been issued on 16th 
November, 2005. These Guidelines are based on the feed back received from 
Hon'ble MPs, the suggestions of the Committees on MPLADS (Lok Sabha and 
Rajya Sabha), the observations made by the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India and the operational experience of the monitoring of the scheme. 
In the revised Guidelines, some of the improvements are as under: 
i) Important sectors like drinking water, education, public health, 
sanitation and roads have been given priority. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
ii) Earmarking of 15% and 7.5% funds for each MP for development of SC 
and ST inhabited areas respectively. 
iii) Automatic release of Rs. 1 crore in respect of MPs at the time of 
constitution of Lok Sabha and election to the Rajya Sabha without 
waiting for monthly progress report. 
iv) Automatic release of first instalment in any financial year in those cases 
where two instalments have been released in the previous year. 
v) The role of Implementing Ag encies, District Authority, State 
Government and Central Government have been listed separately. 
vi) Limit of Rs. 25 lakh of individual work has been removed while 
maintaining the same forTrusts/Societies/NGOs. 
vii) List of the permissible items has been removed. Instead the list of works 
prohibited under MPLADS has been given. 
viii) MPLADS works costing upto Rs. 10 lakh for natural calamities like 
floods, cyclone etc. by MPs from the non-affected areas of their State. 
ix) The maximum limit for rehabilitation of work in the affected areas by 
severe calamities have been raised to Rs. 50 lakh. 
x) A time frame for all the works completed from 1993-94 onward has been 
prescribed for submission of U tilization Certificates and Audit 
Certificates. 
xi) Utilization Certificate for the previous financial year and the Audit 
certificate for the funds utilized in the year prior to the previous year 
have also been made the pre-requisites for the release of the second 
instalment in a year.  
xii) The role of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local bodies as 
Implementing Agencies has been stressed.

INDO-US nuclear agreement 
*31. SHRI MOOLCHAND MEENA: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the first agreement on nuclear  embargo signed in Washington 
with India will help India to develop nuclear policy; 
(b) if so, whether there are many loopholes in this agreement; 
(c) whether this agreement does not rec ognize India as a nuclear weapon 
State nor commits US to sell fuel for Tarapur; 
(d) if so, to what extent this nuclear pact between India and US would be 
helpful; and 
(e) what steps are being taken to implement the agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (e) The understanding on civil nuclear 
energy cooperation set out in the India US Joint Statement issued on July 
18,2005 during the visit of the Prime Minister to the US is significant in the 
context of India's quest for energy secu rity in a cleaner and more efficient 
manner. 
In the Joint Statement of July 18 President Bush conveyed his appreciation 
to the Prime Minister over India's st rong commitment to preventing WMD 
proliferation and agreed that as a responsible state with advanced nuclear 
technology, India should ac quire the same benefits and advantages as other 
such states. The US Presid ent told the Prime Minister that he would work to 
achieve full civil nuclear energy cooperation with India as India realizes its 
goals of promoting nuclear power and achieving energy security. Under the 
Joint Statement the US President 
22 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
would also seek agreement from the US Congress to adjust U.S. laws and 
policies, and the United States will work with friends and allies to adjust 
international regimes to enable full civil nuclear energy cooperation and trade 
with India, including but not limited to expeditious consideration of fuel supplies 
for safeguarded nuclear reactors at Tarapur. 
The implementation of the understanding contained in the Joint Statement 
of July 18,2005 would be helpful in resumption of India securing access to full 
international cooperation in civilian nuclear energy, thereby strengthening 
energy security. 
The implementation of the July 18 Joint Statement would be guided fully 
and entirely by the commitments reflect ed in the Joint Statement only. A 
Working Group to this end, headed by the Foreign Secretary on the Indian side 
and the Under Secretary for Political Affairs of the State Department on the US 
side, has been set up and it held the first meeting in Delhi on October 21, 2005. 
It has been made very clear to the US, induding at the meeting of the Working 
Group that our commitments and obligations would only be those that have 
been spelt out in the July 18 Joint Statement. Each side has expressed its 
perspective on next steps. A road map in this regard is as yet evolving. The 
position spelt out by the Prime Minister, in his statement in Parliament on July 
29, 2005 that our commitments would be conditional upon, and reciprocal to the 
US fulfilling its side of this understanding, makes it clear that we expect a 
close correlation between actions to be taken by the US and India, and that 
Indian actions will be contingent at every stage on actions taken by the other 
side. The two sides are working t ogether closely to implement the 
understanding at the earliest.

Statement 
Brief on TRAI's Recommendations on growth of Telecom Services in 
Rural India 
The recommendations of TRAI provide for a higher quantitative and 
qualitative growth in telecom services in the country, particularly in rural areas. 
Since tele-density is interlinked with the level of development, the large 
differential between rural (1.94 %) and urban tele-density (31.1 %) cannot be 
sustainable. The recommendations state that without focus on rural areas, 
sizeable growth in telecom sector would not be possible. 
As per the TRAI's recommendations, the present USO Policy of 
subsidizing individual DELs, VPTs, MARR replacement, PTICs/HPTICs 
would barely be able to achieve rural tele-density targets of 4% by 2010 even 
after giving huge subsidy support of around Rs. 30,000 crores. 
Recommendations state that such low tele-density in rural areas in 2010 and high 
subsidies to achieve so little can not be acceptable therefore there is a need for 
a re-look at traditional policies regarding the communication needs of rural 
areas and to change these to "Universal Service Opportunity" rather than a 
"Universal Service Obligation". 
TRAI has further recognized some features of the Indian rural market, viz. 
substantial purchasing power at the right price, expansion of broadband/ Internet 
services provided by private sector and the immense popularity 
55 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
of cable TV in India and that such c onnections are far in excess of fixed line 
telephones—a unique feature in the world. It recommends that the proposed 
policy should look at this feature and encourage triple-play networks which 
can be facilitated by Unified Licensing Regime, already recommended by the 
Authority to the Government. 
The Authority has recommended that  an alternative approach of 
facilitating network infrastructure expa nsion should be adopted. This 
approach proposes to offer financial incentives to service providers in the form of 
coverage of partial cost of shared in frastructure and license fee and spectrum 
charge reduction based on the number of rural base station locations. If the 
proposed scheme is implemented early than TRAI's experience of mobile 
growth in urban areas indicate that India would achieve rural tele-density of 
around 15% by December, 2007 and this combined with expected urban tele-
density of around 43% would take the overall tele-density to 22.98% easily 
meeting the target of 250 million subscribers set out by the Hon'ble Minister 
of Communications & IT. If the present USO Policy continues then TRAI 
expects that India would achieve rural tele-density of only around 3% by 2007 
end and in order to achieve the subscriber base target of 250 million it would 
require an urban tele-density of 70% by December, 2007 which is too 
ambitious a target for urban areas and even if achieved would create a much 
larger rural/ urban divide, which cannot be an acceptable policy. 
TRAI has noted that there are already contractual commitments in the present 
USO policy. Accordingly, it recommends that during the validity of these 
agreements both the schemes may work in parallel as there would be balances 
in USOF to fund both, but ultimately only the network infrastructure approach 
should be followed for providing support from the USOF. 
The salient features of TRAI's recommendations are as follows:— 
* Sharing of infrastructure to receive support from USO 
* Supporting backbone infrastructure through USO fund 
* Discount in Annual License Fee and Spectrum Charges linked with Rural 
Coverage. 
* Development of suitable applications 
56 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Reduction of rural VSAT license fees and spectrum charges and 
provision of transponders at affordable rates 
* No right of way charges for networks in rural areas 
* Niche Operators to be supported from USOF and exemption from 
spectrum charges 
* No spectrum fees for usage of CorDECT and similar technologies in 
rural areas as well as for usage of 450 MHz 
* No prior SACFA clearance for deployment of towers upto 40 m. in rural 
areas. 
* Funds collected as Universal Access levy should be made available to 
USOF.

Statement 
Details regarding Competition Commission of India 
Composition: 
The Competition Commission of India (CCI), as provided under the 
Competition Act, 2002, was established on 14-10-2003 comprising a 
Chairperson and 2 to 10 other Members. So far only one Member has been 
appointed in the CCI and full functioning of the Commission has not yet been 
started. 
Main Objective: 
The main objectives of the Commission are to prevent practices having adverse 
effect on competition, to promote and sustain competition in markets, to 
protect the interests of consumers and to ensure freedom of trade carried on by 
participants in market, in India, an d for matters connected therewith or 
incidental thereto. 
Present Status: 
Some of the provisions of the Competition Act and the Selection rules framed 
therein were challenged in Madras High Court and Supreme Court. During the 
hearing before the Supreme Court, Government filed an additional 
71 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
affidavit proposing certain amendments in the Act to meet the concerns raised 
in the Writ Petitions. Consequently, the Supreme Court closed the Writ Petition 
declining to pronounce on the matters argued before it, leaving open all questions 
regarding the validity of the enactment to be decided after the amendment of the 
Act. Accordingly, amendments to the Competition Act are under examination of the 
Government. These are expected to be introduced shortly with appropriate 
approvals. After the amendments are enacted, the Commission would be made 
fully functional.

(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (c) The Civil Nuclear Agreement

Facilities to talented People 
202. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a recen t report by the United Nations 
Development Programme estimates that 100,00 Indian professionals leave the 
country every year to take up jobs in the United States; 
(b) if so, the main driving force for the brain-drain and potential economic losses 
to the country due to this mass migration; and 
(c) what incentives/facilities Government propose to give to our 
exceptionally talented people so that they may stay back in India? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K CHANDRA 
SEKHAR RAO): (a) As per Global Human Development Report 2001 of United 
Nations, about 100,00 Indian Professionals in a year are expected . to take new 
visas recently issued by the United States. 
(b) Most of the students go abroad for higher studies or employment after 
completing their undergraduate studies. Due to high mobility of students and 
scientists accurate estimation of cost of loss to the country as a result of 
emigration to US or any other country is not feasible. 
(c) Several measures have been taken from time to time by the 
Government to minimize the outflow of professionals from various fields 
108 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and also to attract Scientists and technologists settled abroad to return to India. 
Some of these measures are: 
(i) Setting up of more centres of excellence/advanced studies in the 
universities and academic institutions 
(ii) Science and Technology based training for entrepreneurial development 
(iii) Invitation to distinguished men and women of Indian origin settled 
abroad for short term technical assignments to assist in frontier and 
emerging areas of Science and Technology. 
(iv) Increasing the number and amount of fellowships for M.Tech. 
Programme as a result of which, more students have started joining the 
M.Tech Programme. 
(v) Early Faculty Induction Programme which aims at attracting bright and 
young undergraduate students in Engineering and Technology/ 
Pharmacy/Architecture, etc. to take teaching as their career. 
(vi) Appointment of NRIs and persons of Indian Origin in the permanent 
faculty positions in the IITs. 
(vii) IITs have also established In novation and Incubation Centres which 
encourage students to start their own enterprises after graduation. 
(viii) Encouraging graduate students to continue work on sponsored research 
projects which have been funded by various agencies. 
(ix) conduct of counselling sessions for career options of students and taking 
necessary steps for recruitment of students in Indian industries and 
organizations registered in India.

Working Hours for women Employees 
206. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister of LABOUR 
AND EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the prescribed working hours for industrial and other workers; 
(b) whether it is a fact that this norm is not strictly followed in various 
organizations, particularly in private sector financial institutions, resulting in 
exploitation of the workforce and leading to complications relating to mental 
and physical stress, particularly, among female employees; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government would consider issuing directions to all 
organizations to strictly adhere to the working-hours, particularly in respect of 
women employees; and 
(e) if so, by when and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K CHANDRA 
SEKHAR RAO): (a) to (e) As per Section 51 of Factories act, 1948, no adult 
workers shall be required or allowed to work in a factory for more than 48 
hours in any week and Section 54 provide that no adult worker shall be 
required or allowed to work in a factory for more than 9 hours in any day. The 
State Government has the powers to relax or exempt the working hours to the 
reasonable extent. 
Further, as per Section 66 of the Factories act, 1948 no women shall be 
required or allowed to work in any factory except between the hours of 6.00 AM 
and 7.00 PM. The State Government may vary the limits laid 
112 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
down above but so that no such variation shall authorize the employment of any 
woman between the hours 10.00 PM and 5.00 AM. 
Further in the liberalized scenario, though there is no violation of working norms, 
yet, the adjustment/flexibility is being done within the permissible limits.

Human Development Index 
218. SHRIMATI SUKHBUNS KAUR: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact while the number of Indians living in poverty has gone 
down from 35 per cent to 26 per cent during the last decade, India still ranks 
127 out of 177 countries for the second year in a row on the Human 
Development Index of the United Nations; 
(b) if so, what are the determinant norms and criteria laid down, besides basic 
health and education, for determining the index reading; and 
(c) what is the plan of action, if any, for the ensuing decade, for improving India's 
position on the UN Human Development Index, and the targets contemplated 
thereunder? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The number of Indians living in poverty as 
measured by the official methodology of the Government of India has gone 
down from 36 per cent 1993-94 to 26.1 per cent in 1999-2000. India ranks 127 
out of 177 countries as per the Human Development Reports (HDR) 2004 and 
2005 prepared by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). 
130 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) The Human Development Index (HDI) is a summary measure of 
human development. It measures the average achievements in a country 
in three basic dimensions of human development: 
(i) A long and healthy life, as measured by the expectancy at birth. 
(ii) Knowledge, as measured by the adult literacy rate (with two-thirds 
weight) and the combined primary, secondary and tertiar gross 
enrolment ratio (with one-third weight). 
(iii) A decent standard of living, as measured by GDP per capita 
(Purchasing Power Parity US$). Before the HDI itself is calculated, an 
index needs to be created for each of these dimensions. To calculate 
these dimension indices - the life expectancy, education and GDP indices 
- minimum and maximum values (goalposts) are chosen for each 
underlying indictor. Performance in each dimension is expressed as a value 
between 0 and 1. The HDI is then calculated as simple average of the 
dimension indices. 
(c) The Plan of action of the Government to improve the various criteria 
used in the Human Development Index has been incorporated in the Tenth 
Plan document and in the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Plan which 
have been placed in the Parliament Library.

amount of calorie intake out of food consumption along with a

based on the methodology recommended by the Expert Group on 'Estimation of 
Proportion and Number of Poor1 (Lakdawala Committee). The Expert Group, which was

measures including fiscal and financial incentives.

reforms to promote good governance.

with international norms and by rationalizing domestic levies.

and exhibitions, etc.

mechanisms, such as import licensing, safeguards against surge in imports and anti-
dumping measures, to provide reasonable protection to domestic industries, 
including small scale industries.

Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005 has already been

unorganized sector and in keeping with the declaration in the NCMP, a

Schemes for Urban Sanitation 
274. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the percentage of population and households in urban areas devoid of 
toilets facilities; 
(b) the percentage of such population still devoid of drainage facilities; and 
(c) the steps being taken and the Tenth Plan targets in regard to provision of such 
facilities to the urban population in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) As per data submitted by the State Governments, about 37% of 
population in urban areas are devoid of toilet facilities (such as sewerage, 
septic tank or Low Cost Sanitation latrine). About 26.28% households in urban 
areas are devoid of toilet facilities as per data available from Census 2001. 
(b) As per data available from Census 2001, about 22.13% of households in urban 
areas are devoid of drainage facilities (for waste water). 
(c) In order to enhance availability of toilet and drainage facilities for the 
urban population, the Tenth Plan aims to achieve 75% coverage of 
188

urban households with sewerage and sanitation facilities. The Tenth Plan 
document indicates an outlay of Rs. 23,157 crore for urban sewerage and 
sanitation. Ministry of Urban Development is about to launch National Urban 
Renewal Mission and Urban Infrastructure Development Scheme for Small and 
Medium Towns to provide reform-linked assistance to the state governments 
for infrastructure development projects including sewerage and sanitation. 
Schemes to Prevent Flooding of cities 
275. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of URBAN

(a) whether any innovative schemes have been formulated to tide over the 
flooding of cities as it happened in Mumbai, Chennai and Bangalore; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) to (c) Urban sa nitation falls within th e jurisdiction of state 
governments and it is, therefore, the responsibility of the state governments/ urban 
local bodies to plan, design and execute drainage/sewerage schemes. However, 
there is a centrally sponsored scheme of infrastructure development in mega-cities 
viz. Mumbai, Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad and Kolkata to provide assistance 
for infrastructure projects including sewerage and drainage projects in those 
cities. Bangalore Municipal Corporation has informed that re-modelling of all 
primary and secondary storm water drains in Bangalore city has been taken up 
at a total cost of Rs. 400/- Crore. 
Besides, Government is shortly launching National Urban Renewal 
Mission (NURM) for select cities a nd Urban Infrastructure Development 
Scheme for Small and Medium Towns (UIDSSMT) for cities not covered under 
NURM. Storm water drains is one of the eligible components under the above 
mentioned schemes.

Corruption in Hockey Federation of India 
283. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS be pleased to refer to the reply to Starred Question No. 64 given in the 
Rajya Sabha on 28th July, 2005 and state: 
(a) the details of the letter by six Olympians written to him about 
irregularities and corruption in the Hockey Federation of India; 
(b) the action taken thereon; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor and by when action thereon is likely to be taken? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) to (c) Six Olympians had 
written to Hon'ble Prime Minister regarding the functioning; management; 
financial irregularities etc. of the Indian Hockey Federation-(IHF). The Ministry 
examined the issues and senta-detalled response to them. It was informed that 
IHF is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and it is 
autonomous in its functioning. The Government of India only supplements its 
efforts by providing assistance under various schemes of the Ministry and Sports 
Authority of India (SAI). Moreover, 'spor ts' figures in the State list of the 
Constitution and the Central Government does not have the mandate to frame laws on 
any sports related issue. Hence, the guidelines of this Ministry under which 
assistance is provided to recognized NSFs  are administrative in nature without 
requisite legislative backing. Recently, the issue of tenure and management of IHF 
has also been raised in a writ petition filed before the Delhi High Court. The matter 
is still sub-judice. 
Other issues raised by the Olympians included training and other facilities 
given to the hockey players for playing international matches; little pocket 
allowance to hockey players; selection of coaches and managers etc. Here, it 
is mentioned that the Government is providing assistance to IHF for training 
and participation of Indian hockey teams in international events towards passage 
cost with incidentals, board/lodging of team members and other admissible related 
expenses as per entitlement and scale in force. Apart from this, SAI organizes 
coaching camps of 
208 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
national teams. Government of India makes payment for pocket money only for 
tournaments such as Olympics/Asian/Commonwealth Games and the concerned 
NSF is required to make such payment for other exposures out of their own 
resources. Selection of coach and manager is part of the internal functioning of 
IHF. If IHF seeks payment of the rem uneration to coaches, it has to follow 
Government norms for the same. 
As far as the issue of post retirement benefits to hockey players is 
concerned the Ministry has informed the Olympians about the Pension scheme 
for meritorious sports persons being operated by the Ministry. Regarding 
financial irregularities, they have been informed that requisite permission has 
been issued to Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) for audit of accounts of 
NSFs getting assistance exceeding Rs. 1 crore in a year and IHF is one of them. 
Moreover, this Ministry releases the second instalment of assistance of an NSF 
only on submission of audited accounts of the first instalment.

feasible hydro potential in the country. Even with full development of the feasible hydro 
potential in the country, coal would necessarily continue to remain the primary fuel for

department for felling of trees.

hamlets and provide accessibility to el ectricity to all rural households in un-
electrifted and electrified villages in the entire country over a period of four 
years, it is expected that all villages, whether bordering or not, will be covered. 
(c) RGGVY integrates actions to be taken by Government of India, 
State Governments and the utilities so as to expedite the creation of 
electricity infrastructure in rural areas to meet the growing demand for 
electricity required for agriculture, rural industries, health, education and 
IT. The steps taken to expedite RGGVY are:— 
(i) As the existing implementing agencies i.e. State Electricity Boards/ 
Utilities were finding it difficult to accelerate the pace of rural 
electrification, the services of Ce ntral Public Sector Undertakings 
(CPSUs), which have demonstrated their ability in timely project 
execution with effective project management, have been taken, 
224 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
CPSUs have, on the request of State Governments, taken 135 districts 
for rural electrification work under the scheme. 
(ii) DPRs are being prepared district-wise for purpose of cohesirveness and 
better implementation of project. 
(iii) Projects have been taken on turn key basis for effective 
implementation of the project. 
(iv) States have been advised to se t up District Committees with Elected 
Members to monitor the progress of rural electrification work. 
(v) REC has entered into Memorandum of Understaning (MOUs) with 
CPSUs like National Thermal Powe r Corporation Limited (NTPC), 
Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (POWERGRID), National 
Hydro electric Power Corporation Limited (NHPC) and Damodar 
Valley Corporation Limited (DVC) to make available their project 
management expertise and capabilities to states wishing to avail their 
services. CPSUs have taken up work in 135 districts. The list of districts 
assigned to CPSUs is given in the Statement (See below) 
(vi) REC has developed a framework covering the guidelines for 
formulation of projects, procurement guidelines and bidding 
procedure for procurement of goods and services for projects to be 
executed on turn key basis. 
All the states except Goa, which is not participating in the scheme, have 
signed agreement under the scheme. 
(d) The minimum standards prescribed for declaring a village as electrified (under 
new definition of village electrification which is effective form 1st April 2004) 
are as under:— 
(i) Basic infrastructure such as distribution transformer and distribution lines 
are provided in the inhabited locality as well as the dalit basti hamlet 
where it exists. (For electrification through Non-conventional Energy 
Sources a distribution transformer may not be necessary) 
(ii) Electricity is provided to public places like schools, panchayat offices, 
health centres, dispensaries, community centres etc. 
(iii) The number of households electrified should be at least 10% of the total 
number of households in the village. 
(iv) Panchayat has to give the certificate declaring village as electrified.

New Commission to look into Centre-State Relations 
*9. DR. KARAN SINGH: 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY. 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to have a new Commission to deal 
with the issues concerning Centre-State relations; 
(b) if so, to what extent this Commission will be different than the earlier one; 
(c) what are the number of issues that  will be considered by this 
Commission; 
(d) by when this Commission is likely to be formed; and 
(e) by when it is likely to submit its report? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI MANIKRAO GAVIT): (a) to (e) In terms of its commitment made in the 
Common Minimum Programme, the Government has notified on the 30th 
September, 2005 the setting up of a Commission on Centre State relations 
keeping in view the sea-changes that have taken place in the polity and 
economy of India since the Sarkaria Commission last looked at these issues over 
two decades ago. 
2. The terms of reference of the new Commission as compared to the 
Sarkaria Commission are more broad-based. The terms of reference of the 
Sarkaria Commission, which was set up in June, 1983, were as under— 
"The Commission will examine and review the working of the existing 
arrangements between the Union and States in regard to powers, 
functions and responsibilities in all spheres and recommend such 
changes or other measures as may be appropriate. 
In examining and reviewing the working of the existing arrangements 
between the Union and States and making recommendations as to the 
changes and measures needed, the Commission will keep in view the 
social and economic developments that have taken place over the years and 
have due regard to the scheme and of paramount importance for promoting 
the welfare of the people." 
229 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
3. As against the above, the terms of reference of the new Commission are as 
follows: 
(i) The Commission will examine and review the working of the existing 
arrangements between the Union and States as per the Constitution of India, 
the healthy precedents being followed,  various pronouncements of the 
Courts in regard to powers, functi ons and responsibilities in all spheres 
including legislative relations, administrative relations, role of 
governors, emergency provisions, financial relations, economic and 
social planning, Panchayati Raj institutions, sharing of resources; 
including inter-state river water and recommend such changes or other 
measures as may be appropriate keeping in view the practical difficulties. 
(ii) In examining and reviewing the working of the existing arrangements 
between the Union and States and making recommendations as to the 
changes and measures needed, the Commission will keep in view the 
social and economic developments that have taken place over the years 
particularly over the last two decades and have due regard to the scheme 
and framework of the Constitution. Such recommendations would also 
need to address the growing challenges of ensuring good governance for 
promoting the welfare of the people whilst strengthening the unity and 
integrity of the country, and of availing emerging opportunities for 
sustained and rapid economic growth for alleviating poverty and illiteracy 
in the early decades of the new millennium. 
(iii) While examining and making its  recommendations on the above, the 
Commission shall have particular regard, but not limit its mandate to the 
following:— 
(a) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Center vis-a-vis 
States during major and prolonged outbreaks of communal 
violence, caste violence or any other social conflict leading to 
prolonged and escalated violence. 
(b) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States 
in the planning and implementation of the mega projects like the inter-
linking of rivers, that would normally take 15-20 years for 
completion and hinge vitally on the support of the States. 
230 

[24 November, 20051 RAJYA SABHA 
(c) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Center vis-a-vis States 
in promoting effective devolution of powers and autonomy to 
Panchayati Raj Institutions and Local Bodies including the 
Autonomous Bodies under the 6th Schedule of the Constitution within 
a specified period of time. 
(d) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Centre vis-a-vis States 
in promoting the concept and practice of independent planning and 
budgeting at the District level. 
(e) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Center vis-a-vis States 
in linking Central assistance of various kinds with the 
performance of the States. 
(f) The role, responsibility and jurisdiction of the Center in adopting 
approaches and policies based on positive discrimination in favour 
of backward States. 
(g) The impact of the recommendations made by the 8th to 12th Finance 
Commissions on the fiscal relations between the Centre and the States, 
especially the greater dependence of the States on devolution of funds 
from the Centre. 
(h) The need and relevance of separate taxes on the production and on 
the sales of goods and services subsequent to the introduction of 
Value Added Tax regime. 
(i) The need for freeing inter-State trade in order to establish a unified 
and integrated domestic market as also in the context of the 
reluctance of State Governments to adopt the relevant Sarkaria 
Commission's recommendation in chapter XVIII of its report. 
(j) The need for setting up a Central Law Enforcement Agency 
empowered to take up suo moto investigation of crimes having inter-
State and/or international ramifications with serious implications 
on national security. 
(k) The feasibility of a supporting legislation under Article 355 for the 
purpose of suo moto deployment of Central forces in the States if 
and when the situation so demands. 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
4. The Commission shall consist of a full time Chairperson and four full-time 
Members, who are yet to be appointed. No time limit can be fixed as to by when 
the Commission will be fully constituted. It is envisaged that the Commission 
will complete its work and submit its report with recommendations with two 
years. 
Shortage of power 
*10. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is acute shortage of power in the country 
and Government have failed to achieve the target of supplying adequate power 
to various States; 
(b) if so, the details thereof reasons therefore; and 
(c) whether Government are considering strengthening the NTPC for 
generation of more power in various parts of the country and if not, the 
reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED):(a) and (b) There is an 
overall shortage of power in the country presently. The shortage varies from State 
to State and time to time. The average electrical energy shortage in the country 
during the period April—October, 2005 was 7.3% and peak shortage was 9.1%. 
Electricity is a concurrent subject. The supply and distribution of 
electricity in a State is the responsibility of the concerned State 
Government/State Power Utility. The Central Government supplements the 
efforts of State Government by way of generation capacity addition and 
establishment of bulk transmission system in the Central Sector through 
Central Public Sector Undertakings. 
The main reasons for shortage of power are growth in demand outstripping 
the growth in generation capacity addition, shortage of peaking power, low plant 
load factor of some of the thermal generating units, mostly in the State Sector, 
high transmission & distribution losses, shortage of gas and coal, backing 
down of thermal generating units due to better water inflows, prolonged forced 
outages of old plants, poor financial position of most of the State Power utilities 
rendering it difficult for them to raise the 
232 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
resources necessary for making required investments to create adequate 
generation, transmission and distribution system, etc. 
(c) Enchanced delegation of powers (Navaratna Powers) were accorded by 
Government of India to NTPC in July, 1997. As per Navaratna Powers, NTPC 
Board is empowered to inter-alia approve investment in its new/ expansion 
projects without any monetary ceiling. Capacity addition of 9160 MW 
thermal capacity is envisaged to be added by NTPC during 10th plan.

National rural health mission 
†*16.   SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the State-wise number of villages where the National Rural Health 
Mission scheme has been implemented alongwith the date of its 
enforcement; 
(b)the number of villages where female Accredited Social Health Activist have 
been appointed; 
(c) the special measures taken by Government to ensure the presence of 
doctors on duty in village hospitals and the availability of medicines to women; 
and 
(d) the arrangements made by Government for the monitoring of the 
National Rural Health Mission? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) is a strategy to 
bring about architectural correction in the public health sector for the entire 
country with special focus on the States of Bihar, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, 
Chattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Orissa, Rajasthan, Jammu and 
Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura, 
Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram and Sikkim. NRHM is being implemented in atl 
the States as a whole and is especially to address the unmet need of health 
services for the rural poor. The Mission was launched in the entire country on 
12th April, 2005 and was effective in all the states from that date itself. 
(b) Under the strategy of NRHM, 2.5 lakh trained female Accredited 
Social Health Activists (ASHA) at village level are proposed to be engaged 
in ten states by involvement of Pa nchayati Raj Institutions in a phased 
manner over four years. During 2005-06 funds have been released for 
selection and training of one lakh ASHAs in the States of Bihar, Jharkhand, 
Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Orissa, 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
238 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir and Assam. The process of selection and 
training of ASHAs in these states are in progress. 
(c) The provision of services in the Community Health Centres is 
envisaged to be upgraded to the levels of Indian Public Health Standards. The 
IPHS provide for posting of adequate number of doctors including specialist 
in the CHCs. The manpower planning for this purpose is a core activity in the 
process of upgradation of the CHCs to the IPHS. Further, the role of the 
community organisations in monitoring the performance of doctors in the village 
hospitals is envisaged to be institutionalized with the Rogi Kalyan Samitis which 
would increase the accountability in the work of the medical staff posted at the 
hospital. A Task Force has been constituted to examine the feasibility of short 
term courses in medicine for creating a cadre of Health Professionals for rendering 
basic primary Health care and suggest various schemes which would increase the 
availability of doctors in the rural areas. The availability of medicines in the 
Subcentres, PHCs and CHCs is also being augmented as part of upgradation of 
the services in the various primary health facilities in the country. Additional 
drugs including AYUSH medicines are being made available at all the 
centres. A basic drug kits is also being made available to the trained 
Accredited Social Health Activist. 
(d) The NRHM is an umbrella programme of the Ministry which 
subsumes the existing initiatives of the health sector and also seeks to 
introduce intersectoral convergence across other departments of the 
Government. The existing programmes and schemes of the Ministry like the 
RCH II, Vertical Disease Control Programmes, Routine Immunisation etc. are 
incorporated within the Mission. The existing evaluation and monitoring 
protocols of these schemes are being rationalised into a single MIS which will be 
used to monitor the NRHM. The first y ear is the preparatory phase of the 
Mission during which the institutions of the Mission are being put into place. 
The monitoring of progress in this regard is being done through periodic reviews 
and orientation workshops in which the concerned officers of the State 
Government are invited for discussion and follow up. The detailed MIS for the 
Mission is meanwhile being prepared.

*19. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to

244 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) and (b) The National Human Rights 
Commission had taken suo-motu cognizance of the calamity arising from the 
devastating earthquake which hit large areas of Northern India and particularly 
the State of Jammu & Kashmir resulting in unprecedented loss of life and 
property. A team of officials from the National Human Rights Commission visited 
the affected areas of Kashmir for making an assessment about the relief and 
rehabilitation measures being taken. In the light of the assessment made by the 
team, the Commission on 14th October, 2005 made the following 
recommendations:— 
Recommendations made by the Commission 
(i) That with a view to ensure equitable distribution of relief in kind it is 
desirable that the State Governme nt considers having centralized 
collection and distribution centres at  various places in the affected 
areas where relief material could be received from the NGOs, Civil 
Society and other private agencies. The material so received could 
thereafter be distributed equitably to all affected families. 
(ii) Keeping in view that the winter  is already setting-in, the Central 
Government and the State Government should take steps to ensure that 
building material required for repairing damaged property or restoring 
destroyed property is available at the affected places before the access to 
those areas is closed due to winter. This would enable the 
construction/reconstruction of the property to be undertaken at the 
earliest. 
(iii) That since the number of tents required is more than what is physically 
available or immediately procurable despite best efforts of the Central and 
State Governments, it is desirable that where tents cannot be made 
available, temporary shelters in those affected areas are provided to the local 
population so that they may have relief from rain, snow and cold weather. 
These temporary shelters would be there till the buildings damaged or 
destroyed are restored. Essential amenities be provided in these 
temporary shelters for the local population. 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
(iv) The Central and State Governments shall consider feasibility of 
constructing houses in the affected areas with pre-fabricated building material 
which obviously would expedite the job of providing permanent shelters to the 
earthquake victims. 
(v) In all such catastrophes, it is the experience of the Commission that 
children and women are the worst affected. It is, therefore necessary that the 
State Government prepares a computerized list of children who have been 
rendered orphan as also widows and young girls, not only with a view to 
provide rehabilitation to them but also to ensure that their vulnerability is 
not exploited by any one. This computerized list can also assist the 
Government and other agencies, who undertake the task of rehabilitation of 
the orphans/widows/young girls in their task; and 
(vi) Similarly, a computerized list of dead and missing persons be also 
prepared to enable their next of kin to claim proper relief.

(b) whether developed countries are ready to reduce their tariffs on

domestic market and export market; and 
(c) whether India will link the agricultur al issues with Non-Agricultural

48

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) In the on-going 
negotiations on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on 
Agriculture, India has taken the stand that tariff reductions should be made 
from the bound rates on the basis of a tiered formula as provided in the July 2004 
Framework Agreement. The G-20, of which India is a member, favours straight 
linear cuts within tier of the tariff reduction formula, with proportionately lower 
commitments by developing Members as compared with those by developed 
Members. India, along with other Members of the WTO holding similar 
interests and concerns, have demanded that all forms of export subsidies must 
be eliminated by a credible end-date, and all forms of trade-distorting support 
provided by developed countries to their agriculture sector must be substantially 
reduced. India has also taken the stand that a meaningful and operational special 
and differential treatment for developing countries must be an integral part of all 
aspects of the negotiations, including to ensure food security, livelihood 
security and address the rural development needs of their producers through the 
instruments of Special Products and the new Special Safeguard Mechanism 
for developing Members. 
(b) In the negotiations so far, many developed countries have submitted 
proposals to reduce tariffs and domestic support. However, divergences exist 
among various Members in the WTO, inter alia, on the the quantum of 
reductions in tariffs and domestic s upport that should be committed to by 
developed Members and other rules and disciplines applicable on various forms of 
domestic support programmes. It has already been agreed to eliminate all 
forms of export subsidies, though the end-date and other details are still under 
negotiation.

21.      MAULANA OBAIDULLAH KHAN 
AZMI: SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what preparations have been made for the forthcoming WTO 
Ministerial Conference to be held in Hong Kong; 
(b) the countries which are supporting India's stand in WTO; and 
(c) the strategy being devised for effectively putting forth the cause of the 
developing countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.VK.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) India has engaged in these 
negotiations to ensure that its core concerns and interests continue to be 
adequately addressed as negotiations proceed from one stage to the next. On each 
of the issues for negotiations, India has firmed up its position which is 
dictated by its national interests. 
(b) and (c) India has been forming issu e-specific coalitions with different 
countries to ensure that its core concerns and interests find due reflection in the 
negotiated outcome. India is a coordinator of the G-20, a developing country 
alliance, which is actively contributing to all aspects of the agriculture 
negotiations. India has also been a prominent founder member of the G-33, a 
group of 44 developing countries that emphasizes the need for special instruments, 
namely, the special Products and the new Special Safeguard Mechanism (SSM), to 
address their food and livelihood security and rural development needs. In the 
agriculture negotiations, India and Brazil representing the G-20 are members of 
the Five Interesed Parties 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
(Australia, Brazil, EC, India and US). Spearheaded by India, the G-33 has been 
making substantive contribution on Special Products and the SSM. Another such 
example is the Small Group on Services formed to provide impetus to services 
negotiations. The ABI formula, proposed by Argentina, Brazil and India for 
NAMA negotiations are based on the country's present NAMA bound tariff 
average. This formula is backed by the Caribbean countries and some African 
countries. Another important outstanding implementation issue relates to the 
relationship between the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and TRIPS. 
India has been instrumental in forming a group of developing countries (Brazil, 
Cuba, Ecuador, Peru, Thailand, Venezuela, Zambia, Bolivia) for demanding that 
patent applicants should disclose the country and source of origin of any biological 
material or associated traditional knowledge used in their inventions, and the patent 
system should be supportive of the informed consent and benefit sharing 
arrangements that national laws may prescribe. Protection of intellectual property 
rights of private individuals should be supportive of the larger societal interests 
enshrined in the CBD. India is also a prominent member of the Friends of 
Geographical Indications (GIs), a group of more than 50 countries, both developed 
and developing.

47.      SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: 
SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a supers onic fighter jet exposes the pilot to 
Dynamic Gravitation Force which decrease blood pressure in the head which 
can result in loss of vision, blackouts etc.; 
(b) if so, whether the Air Force is thinking of some advanced training 
where the supersonic jet pilots will learn how to handle such a situation 
while air-borne; and 
 
(c) whether Air Force have developed matching combat capabilities 
in view of the high profile Air Force operating in our neighbouring 
countries? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE). (a) The 
pilot/aircrew of supersonic fighter jets are subjected to acceleration forces(G) 
during certain air combat manoeuvres/aerobatics. This can lead to decreased 
perfusion of blood to the eyes and brain which in turn causes tunneling of vision, 
black out or loss of consciousness. 
(b) The pilots of the Indian Air Force are trained adequately at the Institute of 
Aerospace Medicine, Bangalore and are taught to counter acceleration forces due 
to gravity. The pilots wear an anti 'G' suit which also provides additional 
protection against acceleration due to gravity. 
(c) The capabilities of Indian Air Force pilots to combat the ill effects of these 
accelerative forces during air combat manoeuvres/aerobatics are at par with those 
of out neighbouring/other countries.

310 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 against them. Subsequently, in exercise of

(a) The jail staff are being frequently rota ted at all levels in different jails 
periodically so as to minimize vested interests.

(b) what are the terms of reference initiated before enacting the law;

to serve the purpose;

Commission and view of State Governments will be considered; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI SHRIPRAKASH JAISWAL): (a) to (d) A Committee of experts has 
been constituted on 20/09/05 to draft a new Police Act to replace the Police 
Act of 1861. The said Committee has been asked to submit its report within a 
period of six months. The terms of reference of the Committee are as under: - 
(i) To examine the Model Police Act prepared by National Police 
Commission and other draft Model Police Acts and suggest 
modifications as per the changing role/responsibilities of police in view 
of the new challenges before it, specially growth and spread of 
insurgency/militancy/naxalism etc. 
(ii) To suggest measures for attitudinal changes of police including working 
methodology, to elicit cooperation and assistance of the community rather 
than its distrust. 
(iii) The new Police Act should reflect expectation of the people regarding the 
police in a democratic setup. 
(iv) It should emphasise the use of scientific investigation methods to 
strengthen the criminal justice system. It should enable the police to 
tackle futuristic trends of organized crimes including cyber crimes and 
technological advantages in the hands of the criminals. 
(v) The concern for human rights, weaker sections, women and the people 
belonging to scheduled caste/scheduled tribes have to be addressed.

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA

National Police Commission and the views of the State Governments. Views of 
the State Governments have already been sought in this regard.

investment, better training and capacity building is required. This involves up-
gradation in communications, weaponry, forensic setup, transport and improving 
the quality of investigation. However, Police being an entry in the State List of 
the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, the State Governments have the 
primary responsibility to control crime and respond to new challenges of law and 
order situation. The Central Government has been assisting the State 
Governments for modernization of their police forces, for raising India Reserve 
Battalions and also providing Central Paramilitary Forces to face the emergent 
challenges.

Areas affected in recent earthquake 
76. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the areas affected by the recent earthquake, state-wise; 
(b) the number of persons died in the earthquake; state-wise; 
(c) whether Union Government are taking steps for the rehabilitation of the 
persons affected by the earthquake; 
(d) if so, the details thereof, State-wise; 
(e) whether Union Government propose to provide assistance to States in 
constructing quake proof houses/school buildings in quake prone areas; 
(0 if so, the details thereof, State-wise; and 
(g) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) and (b) An earthquake of an intensity of 7.4 on 
the Richter scale occurred on 8th October, 2005 at 0920 hours. The epicenter 
of the Earthquake was in Pakistan, 55 KMs west-North West of Muzaffarabad. 
Tremors of the earthquake were felt in several States of Northern India which 
inter-alia includes the States of Jammu & kashmir, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, 
Haryana, Delhi, Rajasthan and Uttranchal. 
The State of Jammu & Kashmir was the worst affected. AS per provisional figures 
received from the State Governments of J & K and Punjab, 1336 persons are 
reported to have lost their lives in Jammu and Kashmir and 2 persons in the 
Punjab. No other State has reported loss of human lives due to this 
earthquake. 
(c) to (g) As per the existing Scheme for financing Relief Expenditure, the 
State Government concerned is the first responder to the disaster situation and 
is primarily responsible for undertakin g necessary relief measures in the 
wake of natural disasters and for distribution of relief material on the ground. 
The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Governments by 
providing financial and logistic support, wherever necessary. The State 
Governments are required to undertake relief and rehabilitation measures in the 
calamity affected areas out of the 
314 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
corpus of the State Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), in accordance with approved items 
and norms of assistance. The CRF is contributed by the Government of India and the 
State Govt. in the ratio of 3:1. Additional financial assistance is also provided from 
the National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF) in the wake of a calamity of a 
severe nature, after following the laid down procedure. 
The State Government of Jammu & Kashmir has informed that they have 
undertaken necessary relief and rehabilitation measures in the affected areas which 
include provision of tents, temporary shelter, foodgrains, woolen clothes, utensils, 
medicines etc. Financial assistance has also been provided for repair/reconstruction 
of damaged houses, ex-gratia to the families of deceased etc. 
The State Government has announced a financial assistance of Rs. 1.00 
lakh each of the affected families, whose houses were fully damaged, for the 
reconstruction of their damaged houses on their own. The distribution of first 
installment of 40% of the said amount i.e.Rs.40,000/ - to each such beneficiary had 
already started with effect from 19.10.2005. 
Apart from above, the State Government has also decided to construct 22,000 
Temporary Shelter Units (TSUs) (15,000 in Uri and 7,000 in Tangdhar) for 
those families whose houses have been fully damaged. Some of these shelters for the 
hapless families are proposed to be constructed by the Government, while the 
remaining shelters are being constructed by the affected families themselves for 
which the State Government has decided to provide assistance of Rs. 30,000. 
The State Government has also announced an incentive of Rs.5000/- to those 
families who are able to construct TSUs before November 30,2005. Engineers 
and masons have also been trained for assisting the people in the construction of 
earthquake proof houses/buildings. 
The Government of India has provide all necessary financial and logistical support 
required by the Government of Jammu & Kashmir. This includes the supply of 
tents, tarpaulin sheets, sleeping bags, mattresses, blankets, woolens, medicines etc. 
In additbn, Government of India has also provided CGI sheets for construction 
of temporary shelters. 
The Union Ministry of Urban Development has proposed to construct 130 
Community Halls in 130 locations (Uri-66, Tangdhar-38 and Poonch-26. Each 
Community Hall has the capacity to accommodate 150-200 
315 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
persons. The Ministry of Urban Development has also constructed Building 
Demonstration Centers at Uri and Tangdhar for disseminating knowledge on best 
construction practices in earthquake prone areas. 
As a part of the overall rehabilitation effort, various agencies of the 
Government of India have adopted 22 villages, wherein these agencies propose 
to construct shelters and provide other amenities to meet the short-term and 
long-term needs of the affected people. Technical guidance is also being provided 
for the construction of earthquake resistance structures. 
The Emergency Support line Central Ministries/Departments viz. Health and 
Family Welfare, Food and Public Distribution, Petroleum and Natural Gas, 
Urban Development, Drinking Water Supply, Telecommunication, Road 
Transport & Highways, Animal Husbandry, Women & Child Development, 
Power, Civil Aviation, Railways etc. have also provided the necessary relief and 
rehabilitation assistance, as required by the State Government.

Development of hydro-power potential 
93. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that there is hydro-power potential of more than 
1,50,000 MW of which nearly 80 per cent is still to be developed; 
(b) if so, what are the constraints in fully utilizing this potential of energy; 
(c) when the 162 schemes where pre-feasibility reports have been prepared will 
be implemented; and 
(d) what is the perspective planning in the Eleventh Plan for generation of 
hydropower? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The Reassessment 
studies of the hydro-electric potential of the country, completed by the Central Electricity 
Authority in 1987, have placed the economically exploitable hydro potential at 84,044 MW 
at 60% load factor with probable installed capacity in the country as 1,48,701 MW. As 
on 1.11.2005, 28,625 MW capacity (19.2% of the identified potential) has already been 
developed and about 13,380 MW (i.e. 9% of the electrified potential) is under 
construction. The hydro power potential yet to be taken up for development is about 
7f.8% of the identified potential. 
340 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) The main constraints for development of hydro electric potential in 
the country are as under: 
(i) Land acquisition and Rehabilitation problems. 
(ii) Environment, Forest and Wildlife Clearance Problems. 
(iii) Adverse Geological Problems. 
(iv) Location of hydro sites in remote & inhospitable areas. 
(v) Law & Order Problems. 
(vi) Inter-State Aspects. 
(vii) Higher initial construction costs.  
(c) Under the 50,000 MW Hydroelectric Initiative, Pre-Feasibility Reports of 
162 schemes located in 16 States have been prepared. Based on a preliminary 
analysis, in the first phase, 77 schemes aggregating to an installed capacity of 
33,951 MW have been taken up for detailed Survey & Investigation and preparatbn 
of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for eventual implementation. These schemes 
are likely to be implemented during 11th Plan and beyond. 
(d) During the 11th Plan, a capacity addition of about 67,000 MW 
(tentative) on all India basis as pe r National Electricity Plan has been 
envisaged of which about 17,000 MW is proposed to be Hydro Capacity.

sign Power Purchase Agreements for this purpose. 
(c) Union Cabinet constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers 
(EGOMs) to consider and decide all issues related to Dabhol Power Project. 
The restructuring framework approved by EGOM inter alia included setting 
up of a 'project SPV having equity contribution of Rs. 500 crore each from 
NTPC, Gas Authority of India Ltd. (GAIL) and Indian Financial Institutions 
(IFIs) to acquire the asserts of Dabhol Power Company (DPC), free of all 
encumbrances and past liabilities th rough the Debt Recovery Tribunal 
(DRT)/Court process. Accordingly, a new Company, Ratnagiri Gas and Power 
Private Ltd. (RGPPL) was incorporated on 8th July, 2005 under the 
Companies Act, 1956 with NTPC and GAIL as promoters. 
Detailed terms and conditions for acquiring the Dabhol Project assets were 
mutually agreed between RGPPL, DPC, Indian Lenders to DPC and other 
related parties and were filed in the Hon'ble High Court of Judicature at 
Mumbai in the Consent Petition on 22nd of September, 2005. On the same day 
the Hon'ble Court passed its Order for the transfer of assets of DPC to RGPPL. 
Thus RGPPL, currently having equity contribution of Rs. 500 crore each from 
NTPC, GAIL, IFIs and non-cash equity of Rs. 265 crore of MSEB Holding 
Company owns the Project and is responsible for its completion. NTPC's role 
in RGPPL is limited to its rights and obligations as one of its shareholder. In 
addition, NTPC, through its consultancy division, is also providing its expert 
technical services for ear ly commissioning of the power plant as required by 
RGPPL on commercial basis.

98. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that consequent upon partial privatization of power 
distribution in different areas in Delh i and New Delhi have resulted in sharp 
disparities in the power-tariff in different parts of the capital; 
(b) if so, the comparative tariff rates for power consumption leviable to 
355 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
different strata of consumers in different areas of the Union Territory including the 
NDMC areas; and 
(c) the steps taken and are being taken to bring about a degree of parity? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) to (c) Tariff for 
various categories of consumers are required to be determined by the State 
Regulatory Commission in accordance with the provisions of the Electricity 
Act, 2003. Accordingly, the tariff rate for various categories of consumers in 
Delhi are determined by the Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission 
(DERC). 
The tariff in NCT of Delhi for the ge ographical areas which are serviced 
by the North Delhi Power Limited (NDPL), BSES Yamuna Power Limited 
(BYPL) and BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (BRPL) are governed by the 
Policy Directions issued by the Government of NCT of Delhi on 22nd 
November, 2001 and 31st may, 2002 in relation to the restructuring of the 
erstwhile Delhi Vidyut Board. Section 14  of the Policy Directions issued by 
the Government vide their notification of 22nd November, 2001 states that as 
a matter of Policy, the Government had decided that retail tariff for the three 
Distribution Licensees shall be identical till the end of 2006-07 i.e. 
consumers of a particular category shall pay the same retail tariffs 
irrespective of their geographical loca tion. These policy directives are not 
applicable in respect of the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) and the 
retain tariff in the NDMC areas is different.

Shortage of electricity in the States 
†101. DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that power projects run by the States in the country 
are not generating electricity as per their installed capacity and due to this there 
is shortage of electricity and its production cost is also increasing; 
(b) if so, the Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any national plan for increasing the 
production by carrying out comprehensive reforms in these projects; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) 
Generation of electricity by the power plants vis-a-vis their installed capacity 
mainly depends on their age which has a correlation with the forced outages 
and performance of the plants. The power generation of State Sector power 
projects during the period April-October, 2005 was about 171,795 Million Unit 
(MU) as against a target of 177,833 MU, representing 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
364 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
a shortfall of about 6038 MU (3.4% of target). The average electrical energy and 
peak shortage in the country during the current year (April-October, 2005) was 
7.3% and 9.1% respectively. 
The cost of generation of power varies from station to station depending upon 
the capital cost, technology used, type of fuel used and size and location of the 
plant. However, with the fixed cost remaining the same, less generation has 
the effect of increasing per unit cost of generation. 
(c) and (d) The following measures have been taken by the Government of India 
for increasing the production in the power plants: 
(i) Providing loan with interest subsidy by Power Finance Corporation to 
States under Accelerated Power Generation and Supply Programme 
(APGSP) for undertaking Renovation, Modernization and Life Extension of 
generating units. 
(ii) Introduction of Partnership in Excellence in plant performance with tie-up 
of better performing power utilities with low performing power stations to 
improve their Plant Load Factor. 
(iii) Reducing period of planned maintenance and adopting better operation 
and maintenance practices.

112. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN:  Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Provision of Urban Amenities in Rural Areas 
(PURA) Scheme is being implemented in 7 States in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (b) Yes, Sir. The Provision of Urban Amenities in Rural 
Areas (PURA) scheme is presently being implemented in 7 States viz. Andhra 
Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Orissa and Uttar Pradesh on

Bio-Diesel produced from 'Jatropha' seeds 
†113. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: W ill the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any action to develop bio-diesel 
produced from 'Jatropha' seeds; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the quantum to alternative fuel estimated to be produced every year; and 
(d) the details of public sector oil companies interested to promote 
'Jatropha' farming by way of giving subsidy and loan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. The Ministry of 
Rural Development has been identified as the nodal ministry for launching the 
National Mission on Bio-Diesel as recommended in the Planning 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
386 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Commission's Report on Development of Bio-fuel. For this purpose, a 
Detailed Project Report (DPR) has b een submitted for the "in-principle 
approval" of the Planning Commission. The DPR proposed a Demonstration Project 
for promotion of Jatropha cultivation in forest and non-forest areas (2.00 lakh ha 
non-forest lands and 2.00 lakh ha forest lands), especially in wastelands, over a 
period of 5 years. 
(c) After stabilization of yield, the seed from the 4 lakh ha Jatropha 
plantations is expected to produce about 4 lakh tons of bio-diesel per year as an 
alternative to petroleum diesel. 
(d) Under the Bio-Diesel Purchase Policy announced by the Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas on 9th October 2005, with effect from 1.1.2006, the 
public sector oil marketing companies will purchase bio-diesel at a uniform 
price of Rs. 25 per litre, which meets the fuel quality standard prescribed by 
the Bureau of Industrial Standa rds (BIS) specification formulated vide 
PCD3(2242)C dated 26.7.2004. The uniform price once fixed shall be in 
operation for six months, at the end of which it would be reviewed. At present, 
the public sector oil companies have no plan to promote Jatropha plantation 
through subsidies and loans on their own.

Making Indian textile industry globally competitive 
118. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have recently decided to aodpt a number of fresh 
measures to make Indian textile industry globally competitive following the 
abolition of Multi-Fibre Arrangement w.e.f. January, 2005. 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) by when the full import of these measures will be perceptible; and 
(d) whether steps have also been taken to protect the interest of labour in the 
textile industry and if so the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA); (a) to 
(c) The Government has been taking a number of steps from time to time to 
make Indian textile industry globally competitive. Some of the important 
initiatives taken are given as under: - 
(i) 100% Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in the textile sector under the 
automatic route. 
(ii) The Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from the SSI sector. 
(iii) The Technology Upgradation F und Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernization and 
upgradation of the sector. 
(iv) To improve the productivity and quality of cotton, Government has 
launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). Incentives are 
provided for better farm practices, quality seeds, improvement in market 
infrastructure and modernisation of ginning and pressing sector. 
391 

RAJYA SABHA [24 November, 2005] 
(v) To Provide the industry with world class infrastructure facilities for 
setting up their textile units, a new scheme namely, scheme for 
Integrated Textile Parks' has been launched by merging existing two 
schemes i.e. Textile Centres Infrastructure Development Scheme 
(TCIDS) and Apparel Parks for Exports Scheme (APES). Government of 
India support under the scheme by way of grant or equity shall be limited 
to 40% of the project cost subject to a ceiling of Rs. 40 Crores. 
(vi) Apparel Park for Exports Scheme (APES)' was launched with the 
obejective of imparting a focused thru st for setting up apparel units of 
international standards at potential growth centres, and to give a fillip to 
exports. Under APES, 12 projects have been sanctioned with an estimated 
support from Government of India of Rs. 191.70 Crores. Against the 
support of Rs. 191.70 Crores, the Government has released Rs.59.46 
Crores so far. 
(vii) For upgrading infrastructure facilities at important textile centres, the 
Textile Centre Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS)' was launched. 
Under TCIDS, 18 projects have been sanctioned with an estimated support 
from Government of India of Rs. 270.80 crores. Of this, the Government 
has released Rs. 52.57crores. 
(viii) The fiscal duty strcuture has been generally rationalized to achieve growth 
and maximum value addition within the country. Except for mandatory 
excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-made staple fibres, the 
whole value addition chain has been given an option of excise exemption. 
(ix) The import of specified textiles and garment machinery items has been 
allowed at a concessional rate of customs duty to encourage investments 
and to make our textile products competitive in the global market. The cost of 
machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy measures. 
(x) For the speedy modernisation of the textile processing sector, 
Government has introduced, w.e.f. 20.4.2005, a credit linked capital subsidy 
scheme @ 10% under TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
(xi) The National Institute for Fa shion Technology (NIFT), its seven 
branches, and the Apparel Training and Design Centres (ATDCs) are running 
various courses/programmes to meet the skilled manpower 
392 

[24 November, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
requirements of the textile industry, especially apparel, in the field of 
design, merchandising and marketing. 
(xii) Facilities like eco-testing laborat ories have been created to enable 
exporters to get garments/textiles pre-tested so that they conform to the 
requirements of the importing countries. 
(d) To protect the interests of labour in the textile industry, a number of steps 
have been taken by the Government such as 'Mahatma Gandhi Bunkar Bima 
Yojana', 'Health Insurance Scheme for Handloom Weavers', 'Group Insurance 
Scheme', 'Group Workshed Scheme', 'Powerloom Service Centres' etc.

122. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state:

drawback rates on garments and restore ad-volarem rate basis failed to enthuse

395

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINGH VAGHELA): 
(a) The All Industry Rates (AIR) of Duty Drawback, 2005-06 were notified vide 
Notification No. 36/2005-Customs (NT) dated 2.5.200$, which came into force
